title: Smallest Covering Interval
statement:
For each query point, find the size of the smallest interval that contains it, or -1 if no interval does.

Contract
- `intervals` and `queries` are non-null and either may be empty. Each interval is a two-element array `{start, end}` with `1 <= start <= end <= 1_000_000_000`; queries are in the same value range.
- An interval contains a point when `start <= point <= end`, so both ends are inclusive. Its size is `end - start + 1`.
- Return an array with one answer per query, in the order the queries were given. Queries may repeat and may come in any order; intervals may repeat or nest.
- Do not modify `intervals` or `queries`.

Examples
- `smallestCovering(new int[][]{{2, 5}, {3, 4}, {8, 9}}, new int[]{4, 6, 9, 1})` returns `[2, -1, 2, -1]`.
- `smallestCovering(new int[][]{{1, 10}}, new int[]{1, 10, 11})` returns `[10, 10, -1]`.
- `smallestCovering(new int[][]{}, new int[]{5})` returns `[-1]`.
hints: Scanning every interval for every query is correct but too slow when both lists are large. Answer the queries in increasing order of value instead.
Sort the intervals by start and the queries by value (remembering original positions). For each query, push every interval that has started into a min-heap keyed by size.

Before reading the heap, pop intervals whose end is before the query; they can never help a later, larger query either. The top of the heap is then the answer. Intended complexity: O((n + q) log (n + q)) time for n intervals and q queries, and O(n + q) extra space.
inputSyntax: Input: intervals, a bar, then queries, for example: [[2,5],[3,4],[8,9]] | [4,6,9,1]
